hints: Look closely at cell C. See the two small grey blocks at the top and bottom of its wall and how the outer arrows stop there.
Remember which root layer has a waterproof Casparian strip that blocks the apoplast pathway and forces all water into the living cytoplasm.
walkthrough:
**Spot the two water pathways**

Look at the arrows. The outer arrows going around the cells are the apoplast pathway in the cell walls. The middle arrows going straight through the cells are the symplast pathway through the cytoplasm and plasmodesmata.

Notice that in cells A and B, both pathways flow freely from left to right.

**Find where the outer pathway is blocked**

Now look at cell C. It has dark grey patches in its top and bottom walls. The outer apoplast arrows cannot get past them and are forced to turn inward into the cell, as the small diagonal arrows show.

This waterproof block is the Casparian strip, made of suberin.

**Link the Casparian strip to the endodermis**

Only one layer in the root has the Casparian strip, and that is the endodermis. Its job is to act as a checkpoint, forcing water and minerals out of the dead walls and into living cells for selective control.

Since cell C is the one showing this block, cell C must be in the endodermis.

options.A: Cell A is the outermost cell, likely a root hair or epidermal cell, where water is just entering by both apoplast and symplast with no block.
options.B: Cell B is a cortex cell. Both the apoplast and symplast pathways pass straight through it, so it has no Casparian strip.
options.C: Cell C shows the Casparian strip blocking the apoplast and diverting water into the symplast. This is the defining feature of an endodermal cell.
options.D: Cell D is inside the endodermis, closest to the xylem (pericycle region). Water has already passed the checkpoint, so no block is seen here.
